pos: adv. (on board a ship; used once, of Paul's company boarding at Patara)
etymology: English a- (on) + board, the side or deck of a vessel, from Old English bord. It renders no distinct Greek word at Acts 21:2 but translates the verb of embarking.
biblical_def:
Luke's travel narrative is one of the plainest passages of seamanship in ancient literature, and the word occurs in the middle of it: And finding a ship sailing over unto Phenicia, we went aboard, and set forth. Paul is going up to Jerusalem knowing what waits for him there, and the sentence has not a trace of drama in it. They found a ship; they went aboard; they set forth. The Holy Ghost preserved the itinerary — Coos, Rhodes, Patara, Cyprus on the left hand, Tyre to unload — because the gospel travelled by ordinary means, on working vessels, with cargo in the hold.

What follows at Tyre gives the whole passage its weight. The disciples there said to Paul through the Spirit, that he should not go up to Jerusalem; and when the week was out they all came with wives and children to the shore, and knelt on the sand, and prayed, and Paul went aboard again. He was not disobeying the Spirit. He had already told them he went bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing what should befall him there, and later said plainly that he was ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. The believers read the Spirit's warning as a prohibition; the apostle received it as preparation. It is a rare and useful picture of how the same true revelation may be rightly given and wrongly applied, and of a man going aboard anyway.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): within a ship, vessel or boat; on board.
webster_full: ABOARD, adv. Within a ship, vessel or boat; on board.
BOARD, n. The deck of a ship; hence, the ship itself.
EMBARK, v.i. To go on board of a ship or boat; to enter upon a voyage.
VESSEL, n. Any building used in navigation, of any kind or size.
SHORE, n. The coast or land adjacent to the ocean or sea, or to a large lake or river.
scriptures: Acts 21:2
And finding a ship sailing over unto Phenicia, we went aboard, and set forth.
Acts 21:1
And it came to pass, that after we were gotten from them, and had launched, we came with a straight course unto Coos, and the day following unto Rhodes, and from thence unto Patara:
Acts 21:4
And finding disciples, we tarried there seven days: who said to Paul through the Spirit, that he should not go up to Jerusalem.
Acts 21:5

And when we had accomplished those days, we departed and went our way; and they all brought us on our way, with wives and children, till we were out of the city: and we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed.
corruption_summary: Guidance is treated as a feeling to be obeyed without testing, when Acts 21 shows a true word of the Spirit turned by loving friends into a counsel Paul was right to refuse.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 21:4 is one of the most useful verses in Scripture for anyone who has been told God told me to tell you. The disciples at Tyre spoke through the Spirit — Luke says so — and what they said to Paul was that he should not go up. Agabus at Caesarea does the same thing more vividly with the girdle. Paul goes. He is not rebuked for it, and Luke records no fault in him. The Spirit's revelation was that bonds awaited him; the application — therefore do not go — was the brethren's, added out of love, and it was wrong. Revelation and interpretation are two things, and confusing them has done a great deal of damage in churches where impressions are treated as commands.

The second thing to recover is how ordinary the means were. They found a ship that happened to be sailing to Phoenicia and went aboard. No sign, no fleece, no waiting for a word — a working vessel on its commercial route, and the apostle with his passage paid. Providence in Acts runs almost entirely through such means: a ship, a centurion, a Roman citizenship, a nephew who overhears a plot. A Christian looking for God's leading is generally looking in the wrong place when he looks past the ordinary open door for something more remarkable.
roots_summary: Greek epibaino (G1910), to go up on board; ploion (G4143), a ship; anago (G321), to set forth or launch.
roots_lines: Greek epibaino (G1910) — to step upon, to embark; the verb the AV renders went aboard.
Greek ploion (G4143) — a ship, a working vessel; the common transport of the Mediterranean.
Greek anago (G321) — to lead up, and of ships to put out to sea; rendered set forth and launched.
Greek euthudromeo (G2113) — to run a straight course; used of the run to Coos.
Greek deo (G1210) — to bind; Paul went bound in the spirit to Jerusalem before any chain was on him.
usage: “we went aboard, and set forth” — the gospel travelling by working ship.
“who said to Paul through the Spirit, that he should not go up” — true revelation, wrong application.
“we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed” — a farewell in the sand.

pos: adv. (stranded on the bottom; of the ship that carried Paul, run up on a shoal at Malta)
etymology: English a- (on) + ground. At Acts 27:41 it renders Greek epokello, to drive a ship onto a shore — the AV's only use of the word.
biblical_def:
After fourteen nights driven in Adria, the ship that carried Paul comes to its end: And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves. Luke is exact about what happened to each end of the vessel. The bow drove into the shoal and would not move; the stern took the sea until it came apart. That is the last state of a ship that had been lightened of its tackling, its wheat, and finally its boat — everything thrown over until nothing was left but the hull, and then the hull broken too.

The theology of the chapter is in the two sentences the angel and the apostle contribute. Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee — an absolute promise, every soul spared. And then, when the sailors try to slip away in the boat: Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. The same man who has just declared the outcome certain insists on the means as indispensable, and no one on board is permitted to treat the promise as a reason to stop working. That is the doctrine of God's decree and man's responsibility worked out in a gale, by an apostle, in front of soldiers. The ship is lost, exactly as foretold; the promise is kept to the last man, exactly as foretold: they escaped all safe to land.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): on the ground; stranded; run upon the bottom, as a ship.
webster_full: AGROUND, adv. On the ground; stranded; run ashore, as a ship.
STRAND, v.t. To drive or run aground on the sea shore.
SHOAL, n. A place where the water of a river, lake or sea is shallow; a sand bank.
UNMOVEABLE, a. That cannot be moved from its place; firmly fixed.
VIOLENCE, n. Physical force; strength of action or motion.
scriptures: Acts 27:41
And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.
Acts 27:24
Saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.
Acts 27:31
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
Acts 27:44
And the rest, some on boards, and some on broken pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land.
corruption_summary: Acts 27 is quoted for encouragement and read past the verse that makes it doctrine — the promise absolute, and the means indispensable, in the same paragraph.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors divide this chapter between them. The fatalist reads verse 24 — God hath given thee all them that sail with thee — and concludes that nothing further need be done; the moralist reads verse 31 — except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved — and concludes that the outcome was never certain. Luke will not allow either. Both sentences come from the same apostle, within eight verses, in the same storm, and neither qualifies the other. God ordains the end and He ordains the means, and the means are not decoration on a decree that would have held anyway.

This is the confessional doctrine stated in a gale. God's decree does not take away the liberty or contingency of second causes but rather establishes them, and Acts 27 is the narrative of exactly that: the promise made it certain that every man would live, and it was certain because the sailors stayed aboard, because the soldiers cut the boat loose, because Paul made them eat, because the centurion kept them from killing the prisoners. A believer who uses the sovereignty of God as a reason to slacken has misread the doctrine at the point where the apostle applied it hardest.
roots_summary: Greek epokello (G2027), to drive a ship ashore; prumna (G4403), the stern; prora (G4408), the bow.
roots_lines: Greek epokello (G2027) — to run a vessel aground; used once, at Acts 27:41.
Greek prora (G4408) — the forepart, the bow; what stuck fast and remained unmoveable.
Greek prumna (G4403) — the hinder part, the stern; what the waves broke.
Greek diasozo (G1295) — to bring safely through; the verb of their escape to land.
Greek eutheos / ean me — the conditional of verse 31, except these abide; the means the decree ordained.
usage: “they ran the ship aground” — the end of a vessel already stripped.
“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” — the means, not optional.
“they escaped all safe to land” — the promise kept to the last man.

pos: n. (the principal sail of a ship; hoised to the wind as the crew made for the Malta shore)
etymology: English main (principal) + sail, from Old English segl. At Acts 27:40 it renders Greek artemon, the foresail or artemon of a Roman merchantman — the sail used for steerage in a following wind.
biblical_def:
The last manoeuvre of the voyage is described with the precision of a man who was there: And when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands, and hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore. Four actions in one sentence, in the right order and the right technical vocabulary. Ancient ships steered with two great oars lashed up during the anchoring; the bands had to come off before she would answer. Then one sail, small and forward, enough to give the vessel way and no more, and she runs for the beach.

The phrase in the middle is the one that carries the theology: they committed themselves unto the sea. After fourteen nights of undergirding, lightening, sounding and praying, the seamanship comes down to letting go the anchors and trusting the run. Luke sets that against everything the chapter has already recorded — the centurion who believed the shipmaster rather than Paul, the sailors who tried to escape under pretence of laying out anchors, the soldiers who meant to kill the prisoners. Every human calculation in the narrative fails, and the one word that holds is the angel's. A ship may be handled with all the skill there is and still need a promise under it, and the men on that deck got to shore on both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the principal sail of a ship; the sail bent to the main yard.
webster_full: MAINSAIL, n. The principal sail in a ship; the sail attached to the main-mast.
SAIL, n. A sheet of canvas spread to the wind to impel a ship or boat.
RUDDER, n. The instrument by which a ship is steered; a piece of timber attached to the stern.
ANCHOR, n. An iron instrument for holding a ship at rest in water.
HOISE, v.t. To raise; to lift; to hoist — an older form of the word.
scriptures: Acts 27:40
And when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands, and hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore.
Acts 27:20
And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away.
Acts 27:22
And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship.
Acts 27:14
But not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon.
corruption_summary: The nautical detail of Acts 27 is treated as colour, when its accuracy is one of the plainest evidences that Luke wrote as an eyewitness of real events.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 27 contains more precise seamanship than any other passage in ancient literature outside the technical manuals: the undergirding of the hull, the lowering of gear, the soundings at twenty and fifteen fathoms, the rudder bands, the artemon, the place where two seas met. A reading that files the chapter as edifying legend has to explain why a legend would get the tackle right. The historic Reformed handling of Scripture takes Luke at his word here as everywhere — he wrote as one who had followed all things accurately from the first, and in this chapter he is writing about a night he spent on that deck.

The second thing worth recovering is the phrase itself: they committed themselves unto the sea. It names the moment in any providence when preparation ends and the run begins. The Christian is not excused a single rope of ordinary diligence — the chapter is full of work — but there comes a point at which the anchors come up, and what is under him is not his seamanship. Paul had been given the promise and still ate his bread and gave thanks in front of the whole ship's company. The word held; the mainsail still had to be hoised.
roots_summary: Greek artemon (G736), the foresail; pedalion (G4079), a rudder; agkura (G45), an anchor.
roots_lines: Greek artemon (G736) — the artemon or foresail; used once, rendered mainsail by the AV.
Greek pedalion (G4079) — a rudder or steering oar; the bands of which were loosed.
Greek agkura (G45) — an anchor; four of them were cast out of the stern and then taken up.
Greek eao (G1439) — to let go, to commit; they committed themselves unto the sea.
Greek Eurokludon (G2148) — Euroclydon, the north-easter that drove them for fourteen days.
usage: “hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore” — one sail, enough for steerage.
“they committed themselves unto the sea” — the moment preparation ends.
“there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship” — the word that held.

pos: n. pl. (seamen; in Revelation 18, among the mourners standing afar off from the burning of Babylon)
etymology: From sail, Old English segl. At Revelation 18:17 it renders Greek nautes, a seaman — the root of our word nautical.
biblical_def:
John's vision of the fall of Babylon names three groups of mourners, and the last of them works the water: For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off. Kings, merchants, and then the men who moved the goods. What unites them is not affection for the city but dependence on her trade, and the lament they raise is an accounting: no man buyeth their merchandise any more. They stand afar off for fear of her torment, and they weep for the market.

The phrase in one hour is repeated three times in the chapter, and it is the heart of the warning. The wealth of centuries, the shipping of an empire, the whole apparatus of buying and selling that reached from cinnamon to slaves, and souls of men, is undone inside an hour. James says the same thing to men who plan a year of buying and selling and getting gain, and asks them what their life is — a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. Scripture does not treat seafaring or trade as evil; the virtuous woman is like the merchants' ships, and the Lord Himself taught from a fishing boat. What it treats as fatal is the confidence that a system of commerce is permanent, and the grief of men who discover in an hour that it was not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): mariners; seamen; men whose occupation is to navigate ships.
webster_full: SAILOR, n. A mariner; a seaman; one who follows the seas.
MARINER, n. A seaman or sailor; one whose occupation is to assist in navigating ships.
SHIPMASTER, n. The captain, master or commander of a ship.
MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities bought and sold.
TRADE, n. In a general sense, the act or business of exchanging commodities by barter or purchase.
scriptures: Revelation 18:17
For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off,
Revelation 18:11
And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:
Revelation 18:19

And they cast dust on their heads, and cried, weeping and wailing, saying, Alas, alas, that great city, wherein were made rich all that had ships in the sea by reason of her costliness! for in one hour is she made desolate.
James 4:13
Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:
corruption_summary: Revelation 18 is read as a prophecy chart about a future city and not as the standing verdict on every economy that treats permanence as its birthright.
corruption_paragraphs: Much energy has been spent identifying Babylon with a particular city on a map, and the identification, whichever is chosen, tends to end the reading. The chapter itself is more interested in the merchandise list, which runs from gold and silk and cinnamon down to beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men — a trade that has ended by selling people, filed between livestock and luxury goods. That is the indictment. Wherever an economy arrives at the point of pricing human beings, the sailors' lament is already written for it.

The other half of the warning is directed inward, and John states it as a command in the same chapter: Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues. That is not a call to leave a geography but to leave a way of living — to stop measuring a life by its market position. Men who have done so can hear in one hour without terror. The sailors of verse 17 stood afar off and wept because everything they had was in the freight; a Christian whose treasure is elsewhere may work the same ships and lose nothing that matters when they stop sailing.
roots_summary: Greek nautes (G3492), a seaman; kubernetes (G2942), a shipmaster or pilot; emporos (G1713), a merchant.
roots_lines: Greek nautes (G3492) — a sailor, a seaman; from naus, a ship.
Greek kubernetes (G2942) — a steersman, a shipmaster; the root of our word govern.
Greek emporos (G1713) — a merchant, one who travels to trade; the class that weeps first in Revelation 18.
Greek gomos (G1117) — a cargo, a freight; the list that ends with souls of men.
Greek mia hora (G3391 / G5610) — one hour; repeated three times over the fall of the city.
usage: “every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors” — the men who moved the goods.
“in one hour so great riches is come to nought” — the refrain of the chapter.
“Alas, alas, that great city” — a lament that is really an accounting.

pos: n. pl. (oarsmen; in Ezekiel's lament, the men whose skill carried Tyre out into the water that drowned her)
etymology: From Old English rowan, to row. At Ezekiel 27:26 it renders a Hebrew participle from shut, to row or paddle — the crew of the ship that the chapter has made a figure of the city.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel 27 builds Tyre as a ship, plank by plank — fir from Senir, cedars of Lebanon for masts, oaks of Bashan for oars, fine linen of Egypt for the sail, Zidon and Arvad for mariners, the ancients of Gebal for calkers — and then sinks her in a single verse: Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas. The line is terrible because of what it credits. It was not an enemy that brought her out. It was her own crew, doing their work well. The rowers carried the city into deep water, and the deep water is where the east wind found her.

That is the anatomy of a certain kind of ruin, and Scripture is unsentimental about it. Tyre's wisdom, seamanship, trade, and reach were all real; the chapter spends twenty-five verses admiring them before verse 26 arrives. The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas. The glory and the grave are the same location — the midst of the seas — and the sentence that follows the sinking is thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more. What ruined Tyre was not a defect in her competence. It was that her competence took her further out than she could stand, and there is no verse in the chapter suggesting she was ever warned by her own success.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who row; men who impel a boat or vessel with oars.
webster_full: ROWER, n. One that rows or manages an oar in rowing.
ROW, v.t. To impel, as a boat or vessel, along the surface of water by oars.
OAR, n. An instrument for rowing boats, being a piece of timber round or square at one end, and flat at the other.
CALKER, n. One who calks ships; one who stops the seams of a vessel.
MAST, n. A long, round piece of timber, elevated above the deck of a ship, to support the yards and sails.
scriptures: Ezekiel 27:26
Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas.
Ezekiel 27:25
The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas.
Ezekiel 27:9
The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise.
Ezekiel 27:36
The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more.
corruption_summary: Competence is treated as its own protection, when Ezekiel shows a city carried into the fatal water by the excellence of her own crew.
corruption_paragraphs: The story of Tyre is not the story of a fool. She was, by the chapter's own account, magnificently well run: the best timber, the best craftsmen, the best crews, and a market the ships of Tarshish sang about. The rowers who took her into great waters were doing exactly what they were hired for. That is why the verse should unsettle able men more than lazy ones. Capability extends reach, reach extends exposure, and the east wind is not impressed by seamanship. Proverbs says the same thing in a sentence: Riches profit not in the day of wrath.

The corruption to name is the modern confidence that a sufficiently competent system cannot fail — that enough expertise, enough capital, enough redundancy makes a thing permanent. Ezekiel 28, the chapter immediately following, gives the diagnosis in the prince of Tyre's own words: I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; and the LORD's answer, thou art a man, and not God. That is the whole of it. A city, a company, or a man may be carried by real ability into water that only God can stand in, and the last thing any of them expects is the wind.
roots_summary: Hebrew shut (H7751), to row; mayim rabbim (H4325 / H7227), great waters; ruach qadim (H7307 / H6921), the east wind.
roots_lines: Hebrew shut (H7751) — to row, to paddle; the participle rendered rowers.
Hebrew mayim rabbim (H4325, H7227) — great waters; in the Psalms the figure of overwhelming trouble.
Hebrew ruach qadim (H7307, H6921) — the east wind; the sirocco off the desert, and in Scripture a standing instrument of judgment.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to make strong, to repair; the calkers' work on the seams.
Hebrew qinah (H7015) — a lamentation, a dirge; the form of the whole chapter.
usage: “Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters” — ruin by way of competence.
“made very glorious in the midst of the seas” — the glory and the grave at one address.
“thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more” — the last line of the lament.

pos: adj. (following the sea as a trade; of the men who peopled Tyre before her fall)
etymology: English sea + faring, from Old English faran, to travel. At Ezekiel 26:17 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning from the seas — men whose living came off the water.
biblical_def:
The lamentation over Tyre opens with a question about population: And they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and say to thee, How art thou destroyed, that wast inhabited of seafaring men, the renowned city, which wast strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, which cause their terror to be on all that haunt it! A seafaring city is a particular kind of place. Its people are away more than they are home, its wealth arrives in hulls, and its strength is not a wall but a fleet. Tyre was strong in the sea, which is the strongest thing a city could be in that world, and it is precisely there that the prophet says she will be found destroyed.

The Psalter has a gentler word for the same trade, and it is one of the great passages of Scripture on the sea: They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep. The seafaring man is granted something the landsman never gets — he sees. The psalm takes him through the storm, the mounting up to heaven and going down again to the depths, the reeling to and fro like a drunken man, the crying unto the LORD in his trouble, and then the line that every sailor and every saint knows the taste of: Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven. Ezekiel shows a seafaring city trusting the water; Psalm 107 shows seafaring men crying out of it. The trade is the same and the ends are not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): following the business of a seaman; using the seas; as a seafaring man.
webster_full: SEAFARING, a. Following the business of a seaman; customarily passing at sea.
SEAMAN, n. A sailor; a mariner; a man whose occupation is to assist in navigating ships.
HAVEN, n. A harbor; a port; a bay, recess or inlet of the sea, where ships can ride in safety.
RENOWNED, pp. Famous; celebrated for great achievements; eminent.
DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean.
scriptures: Ezekiel 26:17

And they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and say to thee, How art thou destroyed, that wast inhabited of seafaring men, the renowned city, which wast strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, which cause their terror to be on all that haunt it!
Psalm 107:23
They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;
Psalm 107:24
These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep.
Psalm 107:30
Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven.
corruption_summary: Work at sea — and by extension all hard, ordinary, dangerous labour — is treated as spiritually neutral, when Psalm 107 says it is where men see the works of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: A persistent evangelical instinct locates the spiritual life indoors: in the quiet hour, the study, the meeting. Psalm 107 puts a whole stanza of it on a working deck. They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep. The men doing business are the ones given the sight, and what they see is not a sunset but a storm that brings them to their wits' end and then a calm they did not make. Ordinary labour in dangerous places has always been one of God's schools, and the Reformed doctrine of vocation says so plainly: the sailor at his ropes is as much in his calling as the preacher in his pulpit.

There is no significant postmodern redefinition of this word to rebut. The principle to recover is the shape of the psalm, which is the shape of the Christian life in miniature: they go out, they are lifted and dropped, they reel and stagger, they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, He bringeth them out of their distresses, He maketh the storm a calm, and He brings them to the haven where they would be. Every clause is His doing except the crying. And the psalm ends by asking for the one thing the delivered so often forget: Oh that men would praise the LORD for his goodness.
roots_summary: Hebrew yam (H3220), the sea; mallach (H4419), a mariner or salt; machoz (H4231), a haven; tehom (H8415), the deep.
roots_lines: Hebrew yam (H3220) — the sea; seafaring men is literally men from the seas.
Hebrew mallach (H4419) — a mariner, literally a salt-man; the sailors of Jonah 1 and Ezekiel 27.
Hebrew machoz (H4231) — a haven, a place of refuge; used once, at Psalm 107:30.
Hebrew tehom (H8415) — the deep; where the wonders of the LORD are seen.
Hebrew qinah (H7015) — a lamentation; the form of Ezekiel's oracle over the city.
usage: “inhabited of seafaring men... strong in the sea” — a city whose wall was a fleet.
“These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” — the sight given to working men.
“so he bringeth them unto their desired haven” — the end of the psalm and of the voyage.

pos: n. (a passage by sea; in Acts 27, the one Paul told them would be with hurt and much damage)
etymology: From Old French veiage, from Latin viaticum, provision for a journey, from via, a way. At Acts 27:10 it renders Greek ploos, a sailing.
biblical_def:
Paul had no standing as a seaman and was a prisoner on the ship, and he gave his judgment anyway: Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage, not only of the lading and ship, but also of our lives. Luke records the decision that followed without comment: Nevertheless the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul. The expert and the owner against the prisoner, and the expert and the owner were wrong. Fourteen nights later Paul stands up in the middle of a starving ship's company and says, with no triumph in it, Sirs, ye should have hearkened unto me.

The verse is not in Scripture to embarrass sailors. It is there to show where counsel comes from and how it is received. The centurion's reasoning was entirely sensible: the harbour was not commodious to winter in, the master knew the coast, the owner had the most to lose. What he could not weigh was that one man aboard had been given something the professionals had not. And when the storm came, the same apostle who had warned them became the only man on the ship still functioning — he prayed, he was answered, he told them the whole outcome, he made them eat, and he gave thanks to God in front of all of them before he broke his bread. The voyage was lost exactly as he said. Every life was saved exactly as he said.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a passing by sea or water from one place, port or country to another.
webster_full: VOYAGE, n. A passing by sea or water from one place, port or country to another; a passage by sea.
LADING, n. That which constitutes a load; freight; burden; cargo.
COMMODIOUS, a. Convenient; suitable; fit; proper; advantageous.
ABSTINENCE, n. In general, the act or practice of voluntarily refraining from any action; forbearance of food.
TEMPEST, n. An extensive current of wind, rushing with great velocity and violence.
scriptures: Acts 27:10
And said unto them, Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage, not only of the lading and ship, but also of our lives.
Acts 27:11
Nevertheless the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul.
Acts 27:21
But after long abstinence Paul stood forth in the midst of them, and said, Sirs, ye should have hearkened unto me, and not have loosed from Crete, and to have gained this harm and loss.
Acts 27:22
And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship.
corruption_summary: Expertise is treated as self-authenticating, and the one voice on the ship that had heard from God was outvoted by the two men with the credentials and the capital.
corruption_paragraphs: The centurion's error is the most respectable in the chapter, which is why it deserves naming. He did not despise Paul; he simply weighed a prisoner's opinion against a shipmaster's and an owner's and decided as almost anyone would. Scripture records the decision and then records the fourteen nights. This is not an argument against expertise — the chapter is full of competent seamanship that saves lives, and Paul himself gives practical orders about the boat and the food. It is an argument against treating credential and interest as though they settled a question. The owner had the most to lose by wintering at Fair Havens, and his judgment ran the way his money did.

The believer's use of the passage is not to fancy himself the prophet on every ship. Paul's warning was vindicated because it was true, and he had received it; the chapter gives no licence to override competent people with a hunch. What it does establish is that the counsel of God is not distributed by rank, that a prisoner may be right, and that when a man has been proved right he is to use the standing it gives him the way Paul used his — not to settle scores but to say be of good cheer, and then to hand round the bread.
roots_summary: Greek ploos (G4144), a voyage or sailing; phortion (G5413), lading; naukleros (G3490), the owner of a ship.
roots_lines: Greek ploos (G4144) — a sailing, a voyage; the noun Paul uses of the passage to Italy.
Greek naukleros (G3490) — the ship's owner; one of the two voices the centurion preferred.
Greek kubernetes (G2942) — the shipmaster, the steersman; the other.
Greek hubris (G5196) — injury, damage; rendered hurt in Paul's warning.
Greek euthumeo (G2114) — to be of good cheer; Paul's word after the vindication.
usage: “this voyage will be with hurt and much damage” — a prisoner's judgment, correct.
“the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship” — credential and capital outvoting counsel.
“ye should have hearkened unto me” — said without triumph, and followed by good cheer.

pos: v.t. (to unload a vessel; of the ship at Tyre discharging her burden while Paul waited out the week)
etymology: English un- + lade, from Old English hladan, to load. At Acts 21:3 it renders Greek apophortizomai, to put off a cargo.
biblical_def:
The detail is entirely commercial: Now when we had discovered Cyprus, we left it on the left hand, and sailed into Syria, and landed at Tyre: for there the ship was to unlade her burden. Luke tells us why they stopped — the vessel had freight for Tyre — and that is the only reason given. The apostolic company's itinerary was set by a cargo manifest. Seven days later Paul went aboard again and the narrative moves on toward Jerusalem and the arrest.

The word is worth an entry for what the New Testament does with the idea. The whole vocabulary of burden and unloading is taken up by our Lord and by the apostles for the thing a man cannot put down himself. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest — the burden there is not freight but law, sin, and the weight of a conscience under both. Peter, in a phrase that belongs to the same trade, tells believers to cast all their care upon Him, for He careth for them. And Bunyan, who knew his Bible better than his critics, put the whole doctrine in a picture: the burden rolled from the pilgrim's back at the sight of the cross, and he could not see it again. A ship unlades at the port she was consigned to. A sinner unlades at one place only.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to unload; to take out the cargo of; as, to unlade a ship.
webster_full: UNLADE, v.t. To unload; to take out or remove, as a load or burden.
LADE, v.t. To load; to put on or in, as a burden or freight.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; also, that which is grievous or oppressive.
CARGO, n. The lading or freight of a ship; the goods, merchandise or whatever is conveyed in a ship.
DISCHARGE, v.t. To unload, as a ship; to take out, as a cargo.
scriptures: Acts 21:3
Now when we had discovered Cyprus, we left it on the left hand, and sailed into Syria, and landed at Tyre: for there the ship was to unlade her burden.
Acts 21:5

And when we had accomplished those days, we departed and went our way; and they all brought us on our way, with wives and children, till we were out of the city: and we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed.
Acts 21:2
And finding a ship sailing over unto Phenicia, we went aboard, and set forth.
James 4:13
Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:
corruption_summary: Burden-bearing is offered as a technique — manage it, reframe it, share it — where Scripture offers a Person to bring it to and a place to leave it.
corruption_paragraphs: The common counsel for a loaded life is redistribution: lighten the schedule, set boundaries, share the weight. Some of that is ordinary wisdom, and Scripture has its own version of it — Jethro told Moses to appoint rulers of thousands, and Paul told the Galatians to bear one another's burdens. But there is a burden no committee can carry a corner of, and the New Testament is emphatic about it. Guilt is not a scheduling problem. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden is addressed to a weight the Lord Jesus proposes to take rather than to divide, and the rest He offers is not a lighter load but His own yoke.

There is no significant postmodern redefinition of this word to rebut. The principle to recover is the distinction Galatians 6 makes in two adjacent verses and which English blurs: bear ye one another's burdens — the crushing loads that flatten a man — and yet every man shall bear his own burden, the pack each is answerable for before God. The church exists to do the first. It cannot do the second for anyone. And neither the church nor the man himself can touch the third, the guilt of sin, which unlades at one port only, and where it is put off it is not taken up again.
roots_summary: Greek apophortizomai (G670), to unload a cargo; gomos (G1117), freight; phortion (G5413), a burden; baros (G922), a weight.
roots_lines: Greek apophortizomai (G670) — to discharge a cargo; used once, of the ship at Tyre.
Greek gomos (G1117) — a ship's freight; the same noun used of Babylon's merchandise in Revelation 18.
Greek phortion (G5413) — a burden, a man's own pack; Galatians 6:5 and Matthew 11:30.
Greek baros (G922) — a heavy weight; the burdens believers are to bear for one another in Galatians 6:2.
Greek phortizo (G5412) — to load; the passive gives heavy laden in our Lord's invitation.
usage: “there the ship was to unlade her burden” — an apostle's itinerary set by a cargo.
“all ye that labour and are heavy laden” — the weight He takes rather than divides.
“bear ye one another's burdens” — the load the church can get under.

pos: n. pl. (traders; of Tyre's merchants, called the honourable of the earth just before God stains their glory)
etymology: From Old French trafique, trade. At Isaiah 23:8 it renders a Hebrew participle from kana, Canaan — the Canaanite being so proverbially a merchant that the national name became the trade name.
biblical_def:
Isaiah's burden of Tyre puts the question before it gives the answer: Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth? Two titles in one line, and both are conferred by trade. Her merchants are princes; her traders are the honourable of the earth. In a commercial empire the ranking is done by the ledger, and Isaiah states the fact without irony because the irony is coming in the next verse: The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth.

That is the answer to the question, and it is the only one in Scripture. Who took this counsel against Tyre? The LORD of hosts, and He states His purpose in two verbs — to stain, and to bring into contempt. Note what is in the crosshairs. Not commerce, not ships, not wealth as such; the pride of all glory, and all the honourable of the earth. It is a universal statement wearing a local address. Every system that hands out honour by holdings is under the same purpose, and the Hebrew word behind traffickers makes the point on its own: the trader is called a Canaanite, because in that world the two words had become interchangeable, and a whole nation is remembered in Scripture by the thing it sold.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): traders; those who carry on commerce; merchants who exchange commodities.
webster_full: TRAFFICKER, n. One who traffics or carries on commerce; a trader; a merchant.
TRAFFICK, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling.
MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods.
HONORABLE, a. Illustrious; noble; possessing a high mind; actuated by principles of honor.
STAIN, v.t. To tinge with any different color; to sully; to tarnish; to bring reproach on.
scriptures: Isaiah 23:8
Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth?
Isaiah 23:9
The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth.
Ezekiel 27:36
The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more.
Proverbs 31:14
She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar.
corruption_summary: Trade itself is condemned by some and sanctified by others, while Isaiah's actual target — a society that assigns honour by wealth — goes unnamed by both.
corruption_paragraphs: Two bad readings compete over Isaiah 23. One takes it as a blanket condemnation of commerce, which cannot be sustained: Proverbs 31 praises the virtuous woman precisely by comparing her to the merchants' ships, Solomon traded by sea with Hiram's help, and Scripture everywhere assumes buying, selling and profit. The other reading treats prosperity as evidence of divine favour and quietly exempts the wealthy from the prophets. Isaiah names the actual offence in verse 9 and it is neither: the pride of all glory, and a class called the honourable of the earth for no reason except that they were rich.

What God purposes against that arrangement is stated in a verb of the dyer's trade — to stain. The honour was never fast; He shows it. James applies the identical logic inside the church, where the man with the gold ring and the goodly apparel is seated well and the poor man in vile raiment is told to stand, and calls it becoming judges of evil thoughts. A congregation that seats by income has adopted Tyre's ranking system, and Tyre's ranking system is under a purpose of the LORD of hosts.
roots_summary: Hebrew kena'ani (H3669), a Canaanite and so a merchant; sachar (H5503), to travel about as a trader; nikbad (H3513), honoured.
roots_lines: Hebrew kena'ani (H3669) — a Canaanite; used so often for a trader that the AV renders it traffickers.
Hebrew sachar (H5503) — to go about, and so to trade; the root of the word for merchant.
Hebrew kabad (H3513) — to be heavy, and so to be honoured; the honourable of the earth are the weighty ones.
Hebrew gaon (H1347) — excellency, pride; what the LORD purposes to stain.
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to pollute; the verb rendered stain in Isaiah 23:9.
usage: “whose merchants are princes” — rank assigned by the ledger.
“to stain the pride of all glory” — the purpose, stated in a dyer's verb.
“She is like the merchants' ships” — trade itself commended in Proverbs.

pos: n. pl. (those who trade or deal in goods; in the older English, to occupy is to do business)
etymology: From Latin occupare, to seize or take up. In Tudor English to occupy meant to trade or employ, which is why the AV can say occupy till I come; at Ezekiel 27:27 the noun means the dealers in Tyre's merchandise.
biblical_def:
The sinking of Tyre takes everything down in one list: Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin. The occupiers are the dealers — the men who moved her goods through the market. The older English sense governs the word here and in the parable: to occupy is to trade, to put a thing to work, and the noun is a tradesman rather than a tenant.

That older sense is what makes our Lord's command in Luke 19 so pointed. The nobleman going into a far country delivers ten pounds to ten servants and says, Occupy till I come. Not hold; not guard; trade. The servant condemned in the parable is the one who did nothing wrong except nothing — he kept the pound laid up in a napkin, and his reason was a slander on his master's character: I feared thee, because thou art an austere man. He is judged out of his own mouth. Tyre's occupiers traded brilliantly and went down with the freight because their whole account was in the hull; the servant in the parable would not trade at all and lost what he had. Scripture leaves no room for either the man who trades for himself alone or the man who will not trade because he mistrusts his Lord.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who follow any business; in the older use, traders; those who occupy, that is, employ or trade with, goods.
webster_full: OCCUPIER, n. One who occupies or takes possession; also, one who follows an employment; a trader.
OCCUPY, v.t. To take up; to possess; to employ; to use; to follow, as business; to trade with.
FAIR, n. A stated market in a particular town or city; the wares sold at such a market.
PILOT, n. One who steers a ship; one whose office is to steer a ship into or out of port.
COMPANY, n. A number of persons united for the performance of anything jointly.
scriptures: Ezekiel 27:27

Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin.
Ezekiel 27:9
The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise.
Ezekiel 27:26
Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas.
Ezekiel 27:25
The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas.
corruption_summary: Occupy till I come has been read as a call to hold ground until the rapture, when the English of 1611 means the opposite — put the master's money to work.
corruption_paragraphs: A whole popular eschatology has been built on a mistranslation of a word that has shifted meaning since 1611. Occupy till I come is heard as a garrison order — hold the position, survive until the evacuation — and it has encouraged a Christianity of retreat that regards the world as enemy ground to be held rather than a field to be worked. The Greek is pragmateuomai, to do business, and the parable makes the meaning unmistakable: the servants are judged by what their trading gained. Ezekiel's occupiers of thy merchandise preserves the same sense in a commercial setting.

The corrected reading places a real demand on the Christian. Every gift, every station, every pound is delivered on trust and is to be put to work until the Lord returns, and the parable's condemned servant is condemned for inactivity defended by a wrong view of God — I feared thee, because thou art an austere man. Timidity about God's character produces a napkin. And Tyre stands on the other side as the warning against the opposite error: a city that occupied magnificently for herself, and whose riches, fairs, merchandise, mariners, pilots and dealers went into the midst of the seas together in a single day.
roots_summary: Hebrew arab (H6148), to trade or exchange; ma'arab (H4627), merchandise; Greek pragmateuomai (G4231), to do business.
roots_lines: Hebrew arab (H6148) — to give in pledge, to exchange, and so to trade; the root behind occupiers.
Hebrew ma'arab (H4627) — merchandise, traffic; what the occupiers dealt in.
Hebrew izzabon (H5801) — wares, fairs; the goods of Tyre's market.
Greek pragmateuomai (G4231) — to busy oneself with business, to trade; our Lord's word in Luke 19:13.
Greek soudarion (G4676) — a napkin; where the unprofitable servant kept his pound.
usage: “the occupiers of thy merchandise” — the dealers who moved the goods.
“to occupy thy merchandise” — the older English for trading.
“shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” — the whole trade, together.
